flashcards.q: What is a cascading failure?
flashcards.a: One part's problem takes over a shared resource (workers, connections, a queue) and knocks the healthy parts down one by one.
flashcards.more: It starts small, like one slow API or one slow query. The worker that calls it gets stuck. Once every worker is stuck, even features with nothing to do with the problem go down. Then whoever calls you gets stuck too.

flashcards.q: Why is a slow service more dangerous than a dead one?
flashcards.a: A dead service returns an error at once and the worker is released. A slow service holds workers for a long time until the pool runs out.
flashcards.more: If the connection fails outright, you know within milliseconds that the call failed. But if it connects and the reply arrives 30 seconds later, the worker can do nothing meanwhile. With 2 such calls a second, 20 workers are gone in 10 seconds.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between timeout and max_duration in Symfony HttpClient?
flashcards.a: timeout is the idle limit: how long to wait with no data before giving up. max_duration is the total time limit for the whole call.
flashcards.more: A server that sends a little data every second never trips the idle timeout, which is why you need the total limit too. Without timeout the default is 60 seconds (default_socket_timeout), and without max_duration there is no limit at all. So set both yourself.

flashcards.q: What is the bulkhead pattern?
flashcards.a: Splitting resources into separate compartments so one job or dependency can't take every worker, connection or queue.
flashcards.more: The name comes from the separate compartments in a ship's hull: if one floods, the ship doesn't sink. In software it takes the form of a per-dependency cap on simultaneous calls (a semaphore), separate queues and workers per job type, and a separate PHP-FPM pool for admins.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't PHP's max_execution_time protect workers from a slow API?
flashcards.a: On Linux it counts only the time PHP code is running, not time spent waiting for a network or database reply.
flashcards.more: So even with max_execution_time = 30, a worker can sit waiting on an external API for minute after minute. What stops a worker by the real clock is PHP-FPM's request_terminate_timeout. But that is the last net; the real fix is a timeout on every call.

flashcards.q: How do you choose the timeout for an external API?
flashcards.a: Just above that API's normal slowest reply (p99), and always below your own request's time limit.
flashcards.more: If p99 is 800 ms, 1.5-2 seconds is a good start. Too short and healthy calls fail; too long and workers stay stuck. Always keep inner timeouts shorter than outer ones: HttpClient < PHP-FPM < nginx.

flashcards.q: Why keep payment and report messages on separate Messenger transports?
flashcards.a: So urgent payment messages don't get stuck behind thousands of slow report jobs.
flashcards.more: With everything on one queue, urgent work waits until the slow jobs ahead of it finish. With separate transports, each with its own workers, payments keep moving at their own pace even when the reports queue is full. This is a bulkhead for queues.

flashcards.q: What is the default statement_timeout in PostgreSQL, and what should a web app do?
flashcards.a: The default is 0, meaning unlimited. Put a limit of a few seconds on the web database user, for example 5 seconds.
flashcards.more: Without a limit, one bad query holds both a database connection and a worker. `ALTER ROLE app_web SET statement_timeout = '5s'` limits only that user's queries. Keep a separate user with higher limits for reports or migrations.

flashcards.q: What should a new request do when the bulkhead compartment is full?
flashcards.a: Go back immediately instead of waiting (fail fast), and return a fallback answer.
flashcards.more: Queueing up in front of the compartment brings back the very problem of stuck workers. Symfony Semaphore's acquire() returns false at once when there is no room. Then you show a default value or drop the feature for now: [[resilience/graceful-degradation/whole-page-dies|graceful degradation]].

flashcards.q: How do you choose the limit of a semaphore bulkhead?
flashcards.a: Calls per second × the normal reply time, plus headroom. Too low turns healthy calls away, too high protects nothing.
flashcards.more: At 5 checkouts a second and a 0.2 s reply, about 1 call is in flight at any moment, so 5 slots leaves comfortable room. If the courier slows to 4 s, those 5 slots admit only about 1 call a second and the other 15 workers stay free.

flashcards.q: What is load shedding?
flashcards.a: When more requests arrive than you can handle, turning the extra ones away at the door at once, so the rest are served properly.
flashcards.more: Let everyone in and the line grows, replies arrive after the timeout, and nobody gets served. If you refuse everything above the limit, the requests that got in run at full speed. Tell the ones you turn away when to come back.

flashcards.q: What is back-pressure?
flashcards.a: A full step tells the step before it to slow down, so the crowd doesn't pile up in an invisible line and the pressure goes back to its source.
flashcards.more: For example, when a queue is full the controller returns 503, and the client or upstream service sends less work. The pressure goes back to where the problem is being created. The opposite is silently accepting everything and piling it up inside.

flashcards.q: Why does goodput fall under overload?
flashcards.a: The line gets so long that replies arrive after the user's timeout. The server works hard, but nobody benefits.
flashcards.more: Goodput is the replies users actually got in time. A busy server and finished work are not the same thing. Let in more than your capacity and busyness stays at 100% while goodput drops close to zero.

flashcards.q: What is a bounded queue, and why is an unbounded one dangerous?
flashcards.a: A bounded queue has a fixed maximum size and turns new work away when full. An unbounded one lets wait time, memory and stale work grow without limit.
flashcards.more: An unbounded queue hides the problem: requests keep getting in, so everything looks fine. Meanwhile the wait goes from minutes to hours. Pick the limit like this: limit ÷ worker speed = longest wait.

flashcards.q: When do you return 429, and when 503?
flashcards.a: 429: one client went over its own limit. 503: the server itself is overloaded, and it is nobody's fault alone.
flashcards.more: Rate limiting is personal, shedding is global. In both cases send a Retry-After header, or clients will guess, retry too soon and make the crowd even bigger.

flashcards.q: Why send a Retry-After header?
flashcards.a: It tells the client how many seconds to wait before trying again, so it doesn't guess and retry in quick succession.
flashcards.more: Without Retry-After, a turned-away client sends again immediately, which doubles the crowd. You can give either a number of seconds or a date. With Symfony RateLimiter you can get it from `getRetryAfter()`.

flashcards.q: Which work do you shed first in a crowd, and which never?
flashcards.a: Reports and exports first, then search and recommendations. Payment, checkout, login and health checks are never shed.
flashcards.more: Decide this before the crowd arrives, because in a hurry you will get it wrong. Write the shedding list explicitly in code. Protect most the work that brings in the business's revenue.

flashcards.q: Is a fixed rate cap the same as load shedding?
flashcards.a: No. A fixed cap never looks at the server, so it refuses people even when the server is idle. Shedding refuses work only while the server is overloaded.
flashcards.more: Add an overload signal in front of the cap: load average above about 1.5 per CPU core, busy PHP-FPM workers, a deep queue, or slow replies. While the signal says healthy, serve everything. Once it says overloaded, enforce the cap. The price: a lagging signal and one server judging only itself.

flashcards.q: Why make the shedding decision in kernel.request rather than in a controller?
flashcards.a: A shed request never reaches the database or external APIs, so shedding costs almost nothing and the capacity is saved for important work.
flashcards.more: By the time a request reaches a controller, you have already paid for auth, session and ORM. A listener with an early, high priority avoids those costs. The closer to the door you reject, the cheaper it is.

flashcards.q: What is a retry storm?
flashcards.a: Many clients resending failed calls at once, multiplying the load on a sick service so that it can never recover.
flashcards.more: If 50% of calls fail and each failed call retries 3 times immediately, traffic rises to about 1.9 times. Past the service's capacity it fails even more, and even more retries follow. A minor problem becomes an hours-long disaster.

flashcards.q: What is a partial failure, and why is it harder than a full outage?
flashcards.a: The service is not fully down: some calls fail or are slow. It is hard to spot, and retries sometimes succeed, which adds load.
flashcards.more: A service that is completely down returns an error at once and is easy to understand. A partially failing one answers sometimes and not at other times. So the code thinks "one more try will work," and everyone does it together.

flashcards.q: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
flashcards.a: CLOSED: all calls go through. OPEN: no call goes through, the fallback is returned at once. HALF-OPEN: a few calls are let through as a test.
flashcards.more: It goes from closed to open after several failures in a row. After a while (say 30 seconds) it goes half-open. If the test succeeds it returns to closed, and if it fails it opens again. Just like a fuse: protection first, and a chance to see whether it has recovered afterwards.

flashcards.q: Why is it good to stop calls while the breaker is OPEN?
flashcards.a: Since the call will fail anyway, you return a fallback at once instead of holding a worker for the timeout, and the sick service gets time to recover.
flashcards.more: Two gains at once: your workers stay free (fail fast), and the sick service is relieved of load. Without a breaker, every call drags out to the 2-second timeout and the worker pool runs out quickly.

flashcards.q: What do exponential backoff and jitter each do?
flashcards.a: Backoff lengthens the wait before each retry (500 ms, 1000 ms, 2000 ms). Jitter randomizes that wait so clients don't all come back together.
flashcards.more: With backoff alone, all clients return at the same instant, in repeated waves. Jitter flattens those waves. In Symfony retry_failed you can set both `multiplier` and `jitter` in config.

flashcards.q: Which errors should you retry, and which not?
flashcards.a: Temporary ones: timeout, 429, 502, 503, 504. With 400, 404 and 422 the call itself is wrong, and retrying will never fix it.
flashcards.more: If you retry a POST, send an Idempotency-Key, or the same action may happen twice (such as charging money twice). In Symfony, fix the list of codes with `http_codes`.

flashcards.q: What is a retry budget, and why do you need one?
flashcards.a: A cap on how many retries are allowed, as a small share of total traffic (say 10%). It shuts the door on retry storms.
flashcards.more: With retries at every layer, calls multiply: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. So keep retries in one layer, and stop retrying when the budget's tokens run out. You can add a budget by building a custom RetryStrategyInterface with Symfony RateLimiter.

flashcards.q: Which failures should a circuit breaker count?
flashcards.a: Network errors and 5xx answers: the service is sick. Not 4xx: that means our own request was wrong, and counting it would shut off a healthy service.
flashcards.more: Imagine users keep mistyping a district and the courier answers 404 each time. The courier is fine, but if those 404s counted, 5 typos in a row would cut it off for everyone. In the code, catch only the transport and server exceptions.

flashcards.q: What does a circuit breaker cost you?
flashcards.a: While it is open, users get the fallback even if the service has already recovered. On low traffic it can take hours to reach the threshold.
flashcards.more: A breaker is not free protection. Every open period is a stretch where real users see the degraded answer, so keep openSeconds short, and use a breaker only on calls to remote services that can hang or fail.

flashcards.q: What is graceful degradation?
flashcards.a: When a part breaks, keeping the system up with fewer features rather than shutting it all down, so the most important work carries on.
flashcards.more: Like a home backup battery that runs the fan and lights in a power outage and leaves the AC off. First decide which parts are core (price, cart, payment) and which optional (recommendations, reviews). When an optional part fails, only that part is dropped.

flashcards.q: What is the rule for separating core from optional parts?
flashcards.a: If the task is impossible without it, it is core (price, add to cart). If the task works without it, it is optional (recommendations, reviews).
flashcards.more: Calls for optional parts always go in try/catch, and calls for core parts don't: if a core part is missing, an honest failure is the right answer. Make this split when you write the code, not in the middle of a crisis.

flashcards.q: What are the four steps of the fallback ladder?
flashcards.a: Live data, a stale copy, a default value, and finally the feature off (kill switch). If the upper step isn't available, take the next one down.
flashcards.more: A stale copy is the last good answer, kept in the cache. A default is a safe answer the business approved in advance, such as an empty list. When you switch a feature off, tell the user and give them a way forward.

flashcards.q: For what kind of data must you never serve a stale or invented fallback?
flashcards.a: Balances, stock, prices, payment status and permission checks. A wrong answer there costs money or security.
flashcards.more: An old recommendation list does no harm. But someone who sees an old balance may spend wrongly, and saying "permission check failed, come in" breaks security. In these cases a clear "not possible right now" is correct.

flashcards.q: How do you keep a "last good copy" with Symfony Cache?
flashcards.a: Save every successful answer under its own key with a 24-hour TTL. On failure read that key, and return an empty list if it is missing.
flashcards.more: Give it a separate key so the last good copy isn't lost when a fresh cache entry with a short TTL expires. Sending `degraded: true` with the answer tells the frontend to show an honest note. Log the failures, or stale data could be served for months.

flashcards.q: What is a kill switch, and why should it be changeable without a deploy?
flashcards.a: A switch that turns a running feature off at once. In a crisis there is no time to write new code or deploy.
flashcards.more: It is usually a value in the cache, the database or a feature flag system. If a service gets terribly slow, you can turn the feature off without even calling it. Decide in advance who can change it, and how.

flashcards.q: When do you use Promise.allSettled instead of Promise.all in Vue?
flashcards.a: When several calls are independent and you still need the results of the others even if one fails. allSettled returns each result separately.
flashcards.more: Promise.all throws everything away on the first failure. With allSettled you check which ones were fulfilled and which rejected. Show a full-page error only if the core call was rejected; if an optional one was, drop that part and show a short message.

flashcards.q: What makes a fallback good rather than a lie?
flashcards.a: Decided in advance by the business, visible through a log, metric and alert, and independent of the dependency that failed.
flashcards.more: `catch → return 0` fails all three: nobody approved it, nothing is logged, and it quietly loses money. A better courier fallback is the maximum zone rate, logged and shown to the customer as an estimate.

flashcards.q: Why do old and new code use the database together during a deploy?
flashcards.a: A deploy isn't instant. For a few minutes some servers run the old version and some the new, but they all share the one database.
flashcards.more: In a rolling deploy servers are replaced one at a time, and in blue/green the old environment stays ready for rollback even after the switch. So every release has to be compatible with the old code (backward compatible).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between rolling, blue/green and canary deploys?
flashcards.a: Rolling: replace servers one at a time. Blue/green: switch between two environments. Canary: new version on a small slice first, then everyone if it goes well.
flashcards.more: Rolling is the cheapest but its rollback is slow. In blue/green, rollback is just flipping the switch, though you need double the servers for a while. A canary tests the risk on a small slice of real traffic, but needs good monitoring.

flashcards.q: Which deploy strategy has the fastest rollback?
flashcards.a: Blue/green: the old environment is ready, and flipping the load balancer switch sends traffic straight back.
flashcards.more: In rolling, rollback means another rolling deploy, which takes minutes. In blue/green the switch goes back in seconds. But both environments share one database, so without schema compatibility this doesn't work either.

flashcards.q: What is the expand-contract pattern?
flashcards.a: Splitting a database change over several releases: first add the new thing (expand), then drop the old one once everyone has moved (contract).
flashcards.more: To rename a column: add the new column, release code that writes to both, backfill the old rows, move reads to the new one, and drop the old column in a later release. At every step both the old and new code run.

flashcards.q: Why is the migration that adds a new column made nullable?
flashcards.a: Old code doesn't know the new column exists. If it were NOT NULL, INSERTs from old code would break.
flashcards.more: In PostgreSQL, adding a nullable column with DEFAULT NULL is instant and doesn't lock the table. After the backfill is done, you can add the constraint. On big tables, run the backfill in small batches.

flashcards.q: What are the steps of a graceful shutdown?
flashcards.a: Take it off the load balancer, send the right stop signal, finish work in progress, a time limit, and SIGKILL if it still hasn't stopped.
flashcards.more: A short wait in preStop gives the load balancer time to drop the server. terminationGracePeriodSeconds should be longer than your longest job. A Messenger worker that gets SIGTERM finishes its current message and stops, and a message cut off halfway goes back on the queue.

flashcards.q: Which signal stops php-fpm gracefully, and what does SIGTERM do to it?
flashcards.a: SIGQUIT lets php-fpm finish its current requests, then exit. SIGTERM makes it stop at once, cutting requests in flight.
flashcards.more: Set STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT in the Dockerfile, so Docker and Kubernetes send it instead of SIGTERM. The official php-fpm image already does. A Messenger worker is the opposite: it handles SIGTERM itself and finishes its current message.

flashcards.q: In expand-contract, why must the backfill run after the write-to-both release is fully live?
flashcards.a: Until then, servers on the old code save new rows to phone only. An earlier backfill misses them, and those users show no number once reads move.
flashcards.more: The order is: add the column, release dual-write, wait for the rollout to end, backfill, check that no row has mobile empty and phone filled, then move reads. The backfill copies only rows where mobile is empty, so running it again is harmless.

flashcards.q: Why can you roll code back, but not a database?
flashcards.a: Rolling code back means running the old files again. A dropped column or changed data can't be restored, and down() brings back only the structure, not the data.
flashcards.more: So the safe rule is that migrations only add things (expand), and dropping (contract) happens in a later release. A rollback plan also has: the previous artifact ready, a feature flag, a trigger threshold and a rehearsal.

flashcards.q: What is RPO (Recovery Point Objective)?
flashcards.a: The most data, measured in time, that the business will accept losing in a disaster.
flashcards.more: Everything written since the last backup or replication point is lost in a disaster. With a nightly backup the RPO is 24 hours. For payments you want nearly zero, which takes continuous replication.

flashcards.q: What is RTO (Recovery Time Objective)?
flashcards.a: The longest the business will tolerate between a disaster and the system being back up.
flashcards.more: The clock runs from the disaster until users can work again. Restoring, starting the app and moving DNS are all part of it. If you want a 15-minute RTO, you need a ready region and automatic failover, which raises the cost.

flashcards.q: Who sets RPO and RTO, and why?
flashcards.a: The business, because only it knows what an amount of data or time is worth. The engineer just reports the cost.
flashcards.more: Lower RPO and RTO cost more: an extra region, continuous replication, automatic failover. So don't use one value for everything. Divide by importance: strict for payments, relaxed for reports.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between active-passive and active-active?
flashcards.a: Active-passive: one region works, the other stands ready. Active-active: both regions work, so you have to handle conflicts from writing in two places.
flashcards.more: Active-passive is simple and cheap, but failover takes minutes or hours. Active-active gives a near-zero RTO, but brings data conflicts and much more complexity and cost. For most businesses active-passive is enough.

flashcards.q: What is the pilot light DR option?
flashcards.a: Only the database replica runs in the second region, and the app is switched off. In a disaster you start the app there. Cheaper than warm standby, slower to recover.
flashcards.more: Like a gas stove's small flame: the data stays current, the rest starts on demand. RPO is the replication lag, and RTO is the time to promote the replica and start the app, often 30 minutes to 2 hours. Deploy each release to Region B as well, or the switched-off part rots.

flashcards.q: What is backup-and-restore as a DR option, and what is its catch?
flashcards.a: Copies of the data sit in another region, and everything is rebuilt after a disaster. Cheapest, but RPO and RTO are hours: restoring a big database alone takes hours.
flashcards.more: A 200 GB database restored at 50 GB an hour takes 4 hours before the app even starts. Fine for reports and internal tools that can be down for a day. Not fine when the business needs the site back in an hour or two.

flashcards.q: How do you measure the real RPO in active-passive?
flashcards.a: By the replication lag: how far the replica trails the main database. That much data is lost in a disaster.
flashcards.more: In PostgreSQL, run `SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` on the replica to see the lag. Measure it regularly and set an alert. When the lag is above your RPO target, you are outside the target at that very moment.

flashcards.q: What is a game day?
flashcards.a: On a chosen day, with everyone aware, you cause a failure on purpose and run the entire recovery path, to measure the real RPO and RTO.
flashcards.more: Start in staging, then in production in a controlled way. Write the goal down first, follow the runbook, time everything, list the gaps, and fix them before the next drill. Something will break in the first drill, and that is the gain.

flashcards.q: Why do paper DR plans so often fail?
flashcards.a: Their assumptions were never verified: the backup is in the same place, the restore was never tested, the secrets aren't in the other region, the DNS TTL is huge, the runbook is old.
flashcards.more: On disaster day, these small gaps add hours to the RTO. All of them show up in a game day. So keep backups in a separate region and account, secrets in both places, TTLs short, and the runbook regularly updated.
